front: Equation for the converter in the Contact process
Sources of SO₂ and O₂ for the Contact process
back: SO₂: burning sulfur or roasting sulfide ores. O₂: air.
About 450 °C, 2 atm (200 kPa), vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.

front: Why about 450 °C in the Contact process?
back: Exothermic, so lower temperatures give a higher yield but are too slow (and the catalyst needs about 400 °C); a compromise.

front: Why only about 2 atm in the Contact process?
back: The yield is already very high (over 99%), so high pressure is not worth the cost.

front: Why use excess air in the converter?
back: More oxygen shifts the equilibrium to the right, converting more SO₂.

front: Why are the gases cleaned before the converter?
back: Dust and impurities would poison the catalyst.

front: Why is SO₃ not added directly to water?
back: The reaction is so exothermic that it forms an acid mist that is hard to collect.
Fertilisers (ammonium sulfate, superphosphate), car batteries, detergents, paints, cleaning steel, extracting metals.

front: Environmental impacts of sulfuric acid manufacture
back: Escaping SO₂/SO₃ cause acid rain and breathing problems; spills harm soil and water; heat is recovered.
